# Claim adjudication table

Every claim below was checked against the cited evidence. `Partially supported`
means a kernel of truth exists but the claim as commonly stated overstates it.

| # | Claim | Verdict | What the evidence shows | Sources |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Creatine is an anabolic steroid. | **False** | Creatine is a naturally occurring guanidino compound made from amino acids; it is not a hormone and does not act on androgen receptors. It is not on the WADA prohibited list. | R01, R02 |
| 2 | Creatine damages healthy kidneys. | **False** | Controlled trials and meta-analyses show no impairment of measured GFR. Serum creatinine rises because creatine is metabolised to creatinine, which makes creatinine-based eGFR look worse without kidney injury. | R36, R37, R38, R39 |
| 3 | Creatine causes hair loss. | **Unsupported** | A 2009 crossover trial found higher DHT after loading but never measured hair. A 2025 RCT that measured DHT and hair directly found no difference from placebo. | R43, R44, R02 |
| 4 | Creatine causes dehydration and muscle cramps. | **False** | Controlled trials show no impairment of thermoregulation, sweat rate, or electrolyte balance. Pooled adverse-event data do not show a significant increase in cramping. | R41, R40, R35 |
| 5 | You must load with creatine to get benefits. | **Partially supported** | Loading saturates muscle in about a week; 3 g/day reaches similar saturation in about 28 days. Loading is faster, not more effective in the long run. | R01 |
| 6 | Creatine must be cycled on and off. | **False** | There is no pharmacological rationale for cycling. Continuous use at recommended doses has been studied for years without evidence of harm. | R01, R02 |
| 7 | Creatine HCl is better absorbed, so lower doses work as well. | **Unsupported** | HCl is more soluble, but solubility does not predict muscle uptake. Controlled trials find no advantage over monohydrate at matched or lower doses. | R03, R07, R08 |
| 8 | Buffered creatine is more effective and causes less bloating. | **Unsupported** | A buffered product raised muscle creatine no more than monohydrate and did not reduce side effects. It is monohydrate at a different pH, not a different molecule. | R04 |
| 9 | Creatine ethyl ester is a superior form of creatine. | **False** | CEE degrades to creatinine during digestion, raises serum creatinine more, and produced lower serum creatine than monohydrate in a direct trial. | R05, R06 |
| 10 | Micronized creatine is absorbed better than regular creatine. | **Unsupported** | Micronisation makes finer particles that mix more easily. Tissue uptake is not improved; solubility does not predict muscle creatine retention. | R02, R03 |
| 11 | Creatine builds muscle even without training. | **False** | Without resistance training the pooled effect on lean mass is about zero. Creatine amplifies the response to training; it does not replace it. | R11 |
| 12 | Creatine burns fat. | **Unsupported** | Small reductions in fat mass have been reported alongside resistance training, but creatine is not a fat-loss supplement and the effect is inconsistent. | R12, R16 |
| 13 | Creatine makes everyone smarter. | **Partially supported** | Memory effects are small and most consistent in older adults; the largest young-adult trial found only a small, mostly non-significant signal. | R23, R25, R24 |
| 14 | Creatine is safe for long-term use in healthy people. | **Supported** | Trials up to five years and pooled adverse-event data show a safety profile similar to placebo at recommended doses. | R01, R35 |
| 15 | The weight gained on creatine is fat. | **False** | Early weight gain is largely intracellular water and, over time, lean mass. Fat mass does not increase; some trials show a small decrease. | R40, R34, R12 |
| 16 | Creatine is banned in sport. | **False** | Creatine is not prohibited by WADA. Athletes may still prefer certified products to avoid contamination with banned substances. | R01, R49 |
| 17 | Creatine gummies are equivalent to creatine powder. | **Partially supported** | A gummy can deliver creatine, but independent testing found several products with little or no creatine, elevated creatinine, and a cost several times that of powder. | R46, R47, R48 |
| 18 | More expensive creatine is higher quality. | **False** | Independent testing found no relationship between price and quality; cost per 5 g ranged from about $0.13 to $1.85 for products that passed. | R48 |
| 19 | Creatine is only useful for men. | **False** | Women gain strength and lean mass, particularly with resistance training, and have not shown an increased risk of adverse events. | R21, R22, R19 |
| 20 | Creatine is useless for endurance athletes. | **Partially supported** | There is no clear VO2max or steady-state benefit, but creatine may help with surges, sprints, and high-intensity finishing efforts. | R33, R16 |
| 21 | Creatine prevents injuries. | **Unsupported** | Some trials suggest reduced muscle damage or faster rehabilitation, but there is no evidence that creatine prevents injury. | R01, R16 |
| 22 | Creatine cures depression. | **Unsupported** | Pooled effects are small, below the minimal important difference, and of very low certainty. It is not a treatment for depression. | R26 |
| 23 | Creatine treats concussion and traumatic brain injury. | **Unsupported** | Small trials are promising, but there is no large confirmatory RCT and no clinical guideline for creatine in TBI. | R27, R59 |
| 24 | Creatine is a diuretic. | **False** | Creatine increases intracellular water rather than causing fluid loss; it does not act like a diuretic. | R41, R40 |
| 25 | If you eat meat, creatine supplementation is pointless. | **Partially supported** | Dietary creatine reduces the size of the gain but does not eliminate it; habitual meat intake keeps stores partly saturated, not fully saturated. | R01, R31 |
| 26 | Creatine causes kidney stones. | **Unsupported** | Evidence does not show an increased risk of kidney stones in healthy people at recommended doses. | R36, R40 |
| 27 | Creatine is safe during pregnancy. | **Unsupported** | Human safety data in pregnancy and breastfeeding are insufficient; use requires clinician supervision. | R21, R40 |
| 28 | Only Creapure creatine is pure. | **False** | Creapure is a well-documented German ingredient, but other suppliers also meet compendial purity standards. Ingredient source is not the same as finished-product testing. | R03, R48 |
| 29 | Brain benefits require a much higher dose than muscle benefits. | **Partially supported** | Brain creatine responds less than muscle and may need higher or longer dosing, but the optimal protocol for cognitive outcomes is not established. | R30, R23 |
| 30 | A short ingredient list proves a product is safe. | **False** | Ingredient count says nothing about raw-material purity, heavy metals, or manufacturing controls. Independent testing or certification is the relevant evidence. | R45, R49 |
